summary: Defines a limited common set of Diffserv per-hop behaviors and codepoints for connections between separately operated networks, to simplify configuration and operation.

plainLanguage.summary: Two neighboring companies agree on the same few traffic labels so traffic is treated alike.

questions: what dscp values are used at network interconnections
why remark unknown dscp to cs0
subtitle: Four common Diffserv traffic classes and codepoints for the links between separately run networks.

tldr.problem: Networks that interconnect must agree on which Diffserv classes and codepoints to use. Negotiating this for every interconnection scales poorly, and MPLS Short Pipe tunnels make it hard to carry arbitrary DSCPs edge to edge.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four Treatment Aggregates with fixed PHBs and DSCPs for interconnects. A sender re-marks internal DSCPs to the interconnect ones, and the receiver re-marks them to its own internal values.
tldr.outcome: Mapping to and from the common set is specified once for all interconnections, and unrecognized DSCPs can be re-marked to zero (CS0) unless a further agreement says otherwise.

today: RFC 8100 is an Informational document and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes how to use existing Diffserv mechanisms at interconnections.

sections.title: Why Common Interconnection Classes
sections.content:
Diffserv gives differentiated forwarding based on the Diffserv Codepoint (DSCP) field in the IP header. Many networks re-mark unknown or unexpected DSCPs to zero on arrival. This document defines additional DSCPs that are known and expected at network interconnections, which reduces the amount of traffic re-marked to zero.

The approach, called Diffserv-Intercon, is motivated by providers running MPLS backbones with the Short Pipe Model, but applies to other networks too. Its main benefit is that the mapping to and from the interconnection PHBs and DSCPs is specified once, rather than negotiated and configured separately for each interconnection.

The basic idea is that traffic sent with a Diffserv-Intercon PHB and DSCP is restored to that PHB and DSCP at each interconnection, even if each network uses something different inside. That is only feasible for a small number of DSCPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every pair of neighbours inventing their own labels, everyone uses the same short list at the border.

sections.title: MPLS Short Pipe Model and RFC 5127
sections.content:
With the Short Pipe Model of RFC 3270, penultimate hop popping (PHP) discards the MPLS label carrying the provider's TC field one hop before the tunnel endpoint. No provider TC information is then available at the egress, so the DSCP in the encapsulated IP header must be valid for the provider's network. The IP header cannot carry a different DSCP edge to edge. This is why re-marking unrecognized DSCPs to CS0 is a common practice.

The approach draws on RFC 5127's Treatment Aggregates but differs: DSCPs may differ inside a network from those at interconnects and are restored using the interconnect DSCPs, there are at most two PHBs per aggregate, other PHBs are mapped into the aggregates, and network control traffic is a special case. RFC 5127's Network Control aggregate gives way to a fourth aggregate for VoIP, where even minor glitches are immediately noticeable. MPLS and Ethernet only have 3 bits for TC information, so a small number of aggregates is used.
sections.plainLanguage: In some pipelines the inner label is the only one left at the end, so it has to be one the receiving network understands.

sections.title: The Four Treatment Aggregates
sections.content:
A sending party re-marks DSCPs from internal use to the interconnection codepoints; the receiving party re-marks them to its internal usage. The interconnect SLA defines which DSCPs and PHBs are supported and what happens to unrecognized ones. The four aggregates are:

  • Telephony Service: PHB EF (DSCP 101 110) and VOICE-ADMIT (DSCP 101 100), for the Telephony service class of RFC 4594.
  • Bulk Real-Time: PHB AF41 (DSCP 100 010), for classes such as Broadcast Video, Real-Time Interactive and Multimedia Conferencing, with a rate-based queue.
  • Assured Elastic: PHBs AF31 and AF32 (DSCPs 011 010 and 011 100), with AF31 suggested for signaling. AF33 is reserved for future extension.
  • Default / Elastic: the Default PHB, CS0 (DSCP 000 000). Traffic with unrecognized or unsupported DSCPs may be re-marked to it.

If some PHBs of an AF group (such as AF31, AF32 and AF33 in AF3x) are accepted, other PHBs of that group should not be re-marked outside the group, and in particular not to CS0 unless the whole group is, to avoid unexpected forwarding and reordering.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four lanes: phone calls, big live video, important data and everything else. Everything gets sorted into one of these lanes at the border.

sections.title: Example and Network Control Traffic
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, providers O, W and F peer with provider T. Provider O re-marks its internal AF21 to AF31 at the interconnect. Provider T re-marks the incoming AF31 to its internal AF21 and uses MPLS TC value 2. When the traffic leaves T toward F it is re-marked to AF31, and F maps it to its own internal AF11. The Diffserv-Intercon DSCP is restored at the egress. Traffic from W using CS3 for internal use only, if it leaks across due to misconfiguration, may be re-marked to CS0.

Network control traffic is special. CS6 traffic between networks, such as BGP between two routers on an interconnection link, usually terminates at the ingress node, and operators would agree bilaterally on its use. Under the Short Pipe Model, a provider should limit access to the CS6 and CS7 DSCPs so they are only used for its own network control. Interconnecting carriers should specify treatment of CS6 traffic that is to be forwarded beyond the ingress node, and any other CS6-marked traffic should be re-marked or dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: Each company translates the shared label into its own and back again when passing the parcel on, so the parcel leaves with the label it arrived with.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The DSCP field can expose more traffic classification information at interconnections than using a zero DSCP for everything. If that information is sensitive, the DSCP can be re-marked to zero as a countermeasure, at the cost of losing Diffserv treatment on the interconnect and later networks. With AF PHBs, any such re-marking should respect AF group boundaries.

The document introduces no new features and the Diffserv security considerations in RFC 2475 and RFC 4594 apply. It requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Labels tell outsiders what kind of traffic you send. If that is a secret, you can wipe the labels, but then you lose the special treatment.
